claim: More than 1000 research articles in biology were analyzed for the presence of species names in titles or abstracts.
source: An analysis of more than 1000 research articles in biology reveals that the name of the species being studied is not mentioned in the title or abstract of many articles.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that an analysis was performed on more than 1000 research articles.

claim: The name of the species being studied is not mentioned in the title or abstract of many biology research articles.
source: An analysis of more than 1000 research articles in biology reveals that the name of the species being studied is not mentioned in the title or abstract of many articles.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the analysis of over 1000 articles described in the manuscript.

claim: Data from articles that do not mention species names in titles or abstracts are not easily accessible in the PubMed database.
source: Consequently, such data are not easily accessible in the PubMed database.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the omission of species names, based on inference about how PubMed searches work.

claim: Omissions of species names in titles and abstracts can mislead readers about the true nature of developmental processes.
source: These omissions can mislead readers about the true nature of developmental processes and delay the acceptance of valid species differences.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of omitting species names, based on reasoning about how readers interpret scientific literature.

claim: Omissions of species names in titles and abstracts can delay the acceptance of valid species differences.
source: These omissions can mislead readers about the true nature of developmental processes and delay the acceptance of valid species differences.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of omitting species names in scientific communication.

claim: Journals should require that authors include the name of the species being studied in the title or abstract of submitted papers.
source: To improve the accuracy of the scientific record, I suggest that journals should require that authors include the name of the species being studied in the title or abstract of submitted papers.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings and inferences presented in the manuscript.

claim: Including species names in titles or abstracts would improve the accuracy of the scientific record.
source: To improve the accuracy of the scientific record, I suggest that journals should require that authors include the name of the species being studied in the title or abstract of submitted papers.
evidence: This is an inference about the expected outcome of implementing the proposed recommendation.
